counterexample: The union of 3-colourable subgraphs need not be 3-colourable: K4 is the union of the triangle on {1,2,3} (chromatic number 3) and the star edges from vertex 4 (chromatic number 2), yet chi(K4)=4. Likewise, chi(G-bar)=3 together with chi(boundary G)=3 does not force chi(G)=3, since a 3-colouring of the interior arrangement graph and a 3-colouring of the boundary cycle need not agree across the arcs joining them. Concretely, in this setting the claimed sufficient condition is vacuous: partial G is by definition a 2n-cycle, an even cycle, so chi(partial G)=2<=3 always holds, while chi(G)=3 is exactly the open question being asked. A criterion that is automatically satisfied for every n cannot imply a statement that is not known to hold.
reasoning_summary: Verified in order. Setup (0007) and definitions (0020-0022) are fine: the arrangement graph of n pairwise non-parallel chords in general position in the unit disc, with interior crossing vertices plus 2n boundary vertices, is planar; G-bar is the interior arrangement graph and partial G the boundary 2n-cycle. In 0024 the observation chi(G)>2 is acceptable (such arrangements contain triangles, e.g. an interior crossing point together with two consecutive boundary vertices for n=2), and the citation chi(G-bar)=3 (Felsner-Hurtado-Noy-Streinu 2006) is taken as given. The proof fails at the last sentence of step 0024: 'It suffices to show that chi(partial G)=3 in order to establish that G is 3-colourable.' No justification is given, and the inference is invalid. Knowing that two subgraphs whose union is G are each 3-colourable says nothing about G, because the two colourings need not be compatible on the edges (here, the arcs of the chords running from interior crossings out to the boundary vertices) that join them; there is no argument that a 3-colouring of G-bar can be extended to the boundary, nor that boundary and interior colourings can be reconciled by permuting colour classes. The defect is decisive rather than merely a gap: partial G is an even cycle, hence always 2-chromatic, so the stated sufficient condition holds unconditionally for every arrangement, and if the implication were valid it would settle chi(G)=3 with no content at all. (The subsequent step 0026 compounds this: it deduces only chi(partial G)<=3, which is trivially true, and it also misuses the four-colour theorem, which yields chi(G+x)<=4 rather than =4, and confuses the existence of a 4-colouring of G+x with a bound on colourings of G restricted to the boundary.) The proof's own preface at 0001 concedes precisely this error. Stopping at the first certain failure: step 0024.
